name: Decreasing rest intervals

lead:
Decreasing rest intervals means starting a block with comparatively long rests between sets, such as about 2 minutes, and shrinking them over weeks toward 30 seconds. The idea is to progress by doing the same work in less time.
For appearance, the goal is more muscle and leaner conditioning. Lifters use it as a progression tool alongside adding weight or reps.

paras: People note their rest time on a given exercise and cut it session by session or week by week while keeping the lift and rep goals. It is typically combined with ordinary progressive overload and tracked in a training log.
Shorter rests lower the weight or reps a lifter can manage in later sets, which can affect total training volume. As with any training change, fatigue and technique under fatigue matter.

chain: Work is done in less time or with more total effort
Potentially more stimulus for muscle growth and leaner conditioning
angle.text: Muscle size contributes to physique. Shrinking rest periods is a way lifters add difficulty to a program without adding exercises.

lead: Decreasing rest intervals is a method of progressing a workout by shortening the pause between sets over time, for example from 2 minutes toward 30 seconds. Lifters in training logs on T Nation reference rest-time progression as one of several ways to add challenge [1].

Rest length is an established training variable. A 2009 review of 35 studies found that the rest interval between sets affects both acute responses and chronic adaptations to strength training [2]. A 2010 review of the mechanisms of hypertrophy treats rest as one of the variables that shapes muscle growth [3].

A small randomized trial in 2010 compared constant and decreasing rest intervals for maximal strength and hypertrophy [4], and a 2016 randomized trial in resistance-trained men compared short and long rests and reported that longer rests enhanced strength and hypertrophy [5].

paras: Proponents say shorter rests increase metabolic stress and efficiency, and some report that it is a convenient way to keep making sessions harder. Researchers have examined hormonal responses to very short rests in men [6].

The 2009 review concluded that rest interval length is an important variable affecting both short-term responses and long-term adaptations [2]. A 2016 randomized trial by Schoenfeld and colleagues compared short rest typical of hypertrophy training with longer rests and reported that longer rests enhanced strength and hypertrophy in resistance-trained men [5]. A separate 2010 randomized trial compared constant versus decreasing rest intervals for maximal strength and hypertrophy [4].

Randomized trials in lifters have compared rest-interval strategies, including a constant versus decreasing comparison [4] and short versus long rests [5]. No study has tested a 2 minute to 30 second progression specifically.

lore.intro: T Nation training logs mention rest-time progression among other ways of making workouts harder [1].

claims.claim: Shrinking rest periods over time builds muscle faster
